I am a freshman at Macaulay Honors student at Hunter College pursuing a Human Biology degree with the goal of becoming an oncologist. That experience, combined with my earlier research on environmental causes of cancer at Columbia's Herbert Irving Cancer Center, confirmed that oncology is where I belong. As an Office Coordinator in the Department of Surgery, I am eager to understand how MSK operates at an institutional level while staying close to the clinical mission that drives me. I bring strong organizational and communication skills developed through Student Government leadership, journalism, and community service, and I am committed to contributing meaningfully to a team dedicated to fighting cancer every day.

Radiology is one of the most important parts of oncology and I feel like people don't talk about that enough. I'm a freshman at Hunter Macaulay Honors studying Human Biology and my goal is to become an oncologist. I've interned at Memorial Sloan Kettering before, where I did lung cancer research and got my first real taste of what it means to work in a place that's fighting cancer every day. Working with technologists, learning how patient flow works in a radiology setting, getting comfortable with EMR, that's exactly the kind of foundation I want to build right now.

As an older brother to someone with Down Syndrome, I have often found myself accompanying him to various medical and health appointments over the years. Though the doctors always do their best and are incredibly patient, I often find there is a gap that parents or siblings of the special needs patient must fill. My pursuit of medicine is fueled by my desire to be a doctor who can bridge that gap myself and become a resource to the Down syndrome community.     One of the struggles my family faces in caring for my brother John is getting him to wear his glasses. So much so that we’ve given up on him wearing them at home and now just throw them in his bag to bring to school. We are not alone in this struggle, as refractive error is seen in over 60% of the Down syndrome population, with some studies going as high as 80%. Whether they dislike the weight of the glasses, the texture, or refuse to change their routines, wearing the glasses can be an unavoidable point of conflict. Refractive surgeries provide a solution to many families' struggles, and I believe this internship can be incredibly informative in my journey to bring specialized care to the Down syndrome community.

Imagine packing up a car, renting a hotel, and driving seven hours to see a specialized doctor for a family member with Down Syndrome.     My experiences with my brother John and accounts from other local families have shown me firsthand that this is an ongoing reality for many people in Buffalo, New York. Despite having modern medical facilities like Roswell Park, Buffalo and other underserved communities across the US have abstract needs.    Faced with this reality, parents must make a tough choice: struggle to find a local doctor willing to build a long-term connection or seek out a specialist like Dr. Brian Skotko at Massachusetts General. However, Dr. Skotko has a 10-year waitlist and already serves 600 patients. This wait means that I will likely graduate from medical school before my brother can even schedule an appointment with a specialist. In fact, according to Dr. Skotko himself, if you took all the specialist centers in the United States and maximized their capacity, they would serve five percent of the Down Syndrome population in the United States. This is far from the public perception that numerous resources are available for communities with disabilities like Down Syndrome. It is this disparity in care that motivates me to pursue medicine to address an incredibly underserved community.

Hello, my name is Munachimso Akwitti. I am a sophomore at Bronx Community College studying health science. I am passionate about pursuing an internship in the healthcare field. This passion stems from personal experiences that have deeply impacted me. When I was younger, I tragically lost two of my aunts within two years. Witnessing their struggles and the inadequate healthcare system in my home country, Nigeria, deeply affected me. The lack of access to quality medical care for those not financially privileged and the unconcerned attitude toward health concerns motivated me to dedicate my time and efforts to making a difference in healthcare. This is the reason why I am interested in the CUNY Career Launch.  As a sophomore, I am eager to pursue an internship in a healthcare hub to gain invaluable hands-on experience and deepen my understanding of patient care. As I embark on my nursing education, gaining exposure to different areas of practice will guide my future career decisions. While my coursework provides essential theoretical knowledge, I am conscious that real-world application is crucial for developing clinical skills and confidence in a nursing environment. Interning in a healthcare hub will allow me to observe and participate in the daily operations of a dynamic healthcare organization.  I am particularly interested in how multidisciplinary teams collaborate to provide comprehensive care. Understanding this collaborative approach will enhance my ability to communicate effectively with other healthcare professionals and better serve my future patients. Securing an internship in healthcare is an essential milestone in my pursuit of becoming a skilled and empathetic nurse. This opportunity will furnish me with invaluable experience and profound insights that will propel me toward a successful and fulfilling career in nursing.

As a student in Architecture, with a passion in sustainability, this position would mean a lot to me as there's so much I want to learn about in this field, and I know this job can help me develop into a knowledgeable individual. To me, aspiring to be an architect means being able to hold yourself responsible for the things you create. I feel it’s pivotal for me to gain as much knowledge of the environment around us as possible as what I design can directly impact it in negative ways, and I’d like to minimize that as much as possible. I find this experience to be a lot more than just supplementary knowledge. I want the foundation of my work to be based on methods of sustainability. In my most recent architectural design project, I had to tackle sustainability head-on, as we had to create different pavilions on the site of a nature life preserve. Being as critical as possible in my design, I made sure I visited the site as much as possible to make sure the structure didn’t interfere with old growth trees, and had the space to rest on an area delicately. This project showed me that this type of thought process can apply to any place we design as nature is everywhere. Growing up, my passion for gardening and taking care of plants was strong. I used to look after my family's large fruit garden in my country where we had a lemon tree, peach tree, fig tree, rose bushes, and large grape vines. I’d always wake up early and tend to all the plants the best I could. Now in New York, with the limited space we have in comparison, I still fill my room with many different plants, learning how to nurture each one. I’ve always tried to be proactive and involved in my community through different park clean-ups and shoreline clean-ups. Besides the benefits of learning and growing my knowledge in this field, being able to help out and support our Earth is enough reason for me to join the team.

My journey within the community college system started out rocky. I moved to New York from Paris at 19 years old right after completing my French baccalaureate, with no initial plan on attending college. Thus, when I had finally decided to apply, I found myself unprepared and tangled in endless calls overseas to my family so that I could gather the necessary documents. Following that was a series of administration issues in my admission journey, which had left my academic dreams feeling futile. Yet, when the semester was in motion, I found opportunities that I once believed could only be achieved with wealth and privileges I did not have.    Amidst my regular course load, I spent my semester consistently looking for internships and independent research projects offered by BMCC and I had found what very much felt like a goldmine. I was pleasantly surprised to see intern/research connections to prominent institutions such as Columbia and NYU, which when I had mentioned to many of my peers at BMCC and even other CUNYs, had a startled look on their faces; they were just as unaware of the existence of these incredible opportunities as I once was. I believe there needs to be a better emphasis and guide to research opportunities that are available to community college students. The pipeline from a community college to a private institution such as the Ivy Leagues is one that can seem rather intimidating and unreachable to the many exceptional students at community colleges, especially ones that do not hail from an elite, privileged background. This can demotivate students to even attempt higher education. But the importance of higher education cannot be lost, especially to the students at BMCC, as they represent the exceedingly diversifying walks of life people come from. Thus, if accepted into CCRC, I would utilize it as a foundation to better advocate for my peers to get the academic opportunities they deserve.

Having moved from Paris to New York at 19 years old after finishing my French baccalaureate, I was quickly faced with the differences between countries and culture, how one can influence the other, and also how radical those differences can be.  Since the age of 10, I’ve always been deeply involved in and passionate about creating and sharing ideas, first through YouTube and later through TikTok, where I accumulated 250,000 followers in a year. I’ve learned to become familiar with technological tools, but especially to view social media as a vector for ideas. Majoring in Liberal Arts with a strong emphasis on political science courses, I’ve become increasingly more aware of the influence of politics. Through this combination of interests, Sciences Po would be an ideal environment for me, as it perfectly blends theory with real-world application through public engagement.  This past semester, I was able to conduct a research project focused around the bridge between effective communication strategies and the transmission of ideologies and ideas. This work allowed me to learn how narratives and media shape political discourse; an internship at Sciences Po would allow me to explore those ideas in practice.  Furthermore, my bilingualism and bicultural background are also why I believe I would thrive in an institution like Sciences Po: at a time when cultural differences are increasingly politicized and used as rhetoric, I consider multiculturalism a strength, allowing for a better understanding of perspectives as well as public perception.  Finally, starting my academic journey at a community college such as BMCC made me realize the importance of making international and political environments feel more accessible to students from diverse and/or nontraditional backgrounds. Now more than ever, the challenge lies in adapting new technologies to connect with broader and younger audiences, rather than blaming them for the growing disconnection of the world.

Having moved from Paris to New York at 19 years old after finishing my French baccalaureate, I was quickly faced with the differences between countries and culture, how one can influence the other but also how radical those differences can be.  Early on in my life, comic books and fictional stories often became a source of both solace and entertainment. Although it may seem insignificant, political ideologies have always seeped through within these stories; politics exists even in the most trivial and juvenile of places, molding the perspectives of future generations. This was a simple hypothesis of my own that I got to fully explore and expand upon in my independent research project this past semester, which focused on the Captain America series during politically volatile times such as the Cold War, Watergate Scandal, etc. During my research, I was most fascinated by how societies respond to an untrustworthy government and violations of human rights, reflected by both the writers of these comics and by the way superhero characters act as particularly unique members of law enforcement.   With the current surge of exploitation and genocide in the Middle East/Africa and increasing anti-immigrant rhetoric in the US, I believe the importance of human rights needs to be emphasized now more than ever. Human rights law is one of the very few legal systems that goes beyond borders as it pertains to every single individual. If accepted, with RFK Human Rights as a platform, I’d utilize it as a resource to further both my own and my peers’ understanding of human rights law and advocacy, as we cannot afford to be desensitized to the increasing violation of international human rights law.

For most of my high school years, I was as a content creator and (somehow) ended up with a large audience on TikTok. At the time, I didn’t call it marketing. One weak hook and I would see my watch time reduced to nothing; on the other hand, one well-timed line and I would get hundreds of thousands of views. I learned back then that attention is designed and that small structural choices in the way you speak carry far more impact than people think.    Since moving to New York, communication stopped being performative and started becoming practical. It became a different kind of exercise: I was no longer in control of a language I was born with, and I now had to adapt myself to a new one. But the more comfortable I became with the language, the more strategic my voice became, and the more I learned how to frame it in a powerful way.    Starting my academic journey at a community college as a BMCC student, I have come to realize the importance of making educational and professional environments feel more accessible to students from diverse and nontraditional backgrounds, which is why community and outreach are so important to me.    I feel very drawn to the opportunity to work at CUNY Communications because it would feel like an extension of my years on social media: after doing it mainly for my own ends, being able to share my experience for something much more community-oriented, such as CUNY schools, would at the same time be a new challenge and the perfect opportunity to apply everything I learned throughout those years. Being part of the CUNY system for only a year has made me realize how much it has to offer; I was able to join research programs, student government, scholarships, honors clubs, etc., and that was only at BMCC. I believe new technologies don’t necessarily have to be a weakness: they can sometimes allow genuinely good institutions to make broader and more diverse audiences aware of what they have to offer, and I believe CUNY fits that case perfectly

Having moved from Paris to New York at 19 years old after finishing my French baccalaureate, I was quickly faced with the differences between the two countries and culture, along with how institutions operate and especially offer help in big cities. Within big cities, it is local politics that offers lots of different resources and help , especially for the most sensitive & targeted population that the bigger and broader government simply cannot provide. Even if those two cities— and nations— operate drastically differently, what has been the same  is the importance of democracy and how it pertains to the people of my generation. The responses to politically volatile times in both my time spent in France and the US was a time where I observed my peers engaged in protests, thoughtful voting, rallying, and demands for change to lawmakers. Despite borders and language barriers, the fight for our rights has remained indistinguishable. I believe  that through clear, precise and responsive communication, communities could finally get the help they deserve by becoming aware of the benefits they are getting. Getting the opportunity for work for a direct politician would allow me to enter my first step in my long-desired political career. I would use my voice to present the right resources to more non-traditional communities such as the student body within my own community college. It is easy to overlook community college students in the world of higher education and academia but I believe their judgement is of utmost significance, as they represent a diverse group with unique struggles against class and the status quo; their role in politics is thus undeniable and by extending communication of political resources, I would be a dedicated advocate for one’s pertinent role in the fight for democracy.
